extracted.intended_audience: research integrity community, journal editors, peer reviewers, and scientists concerned with paper mills and publishing quality
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying red flags and suspicious features in manuscripts and published papers that suggest paper‑mill involvement, compromised peer review, or misuse of generative/automated tools. Includes heuristics, examples (nonsense phrases), and detection methods referenced in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fingerprint (recurrent offbeat characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: An offbeat characteristic found in one or more publications that suggests paper‑mill involvement (example: the nonsensical phrase "vegetative electron microscopy").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for odd or idiosyncratic phrases that recur across multiple papers; such 'fingerprints' can indicate a common origin or paper‑mill. The article cites sleuths using fingerprints to identify networks of fake papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstandard or ludicrous phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of wording that is strange, nonstandard, or scientifically nonsensical (e.g., 'vegetative electron microscopy').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag unusual terminology that would stand out even to a non‑specialist; verify whether wording is explained in context or likely the result of mistranslation, machine‑reading artifacts, or AI generation. Presence of such phrases across multiple papers is a stronger red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromised peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the peer review process was compromised for a paper (cited by Springer Nature as a reason for retraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate reviewer identities, reviewer suggestions by authors, rapid acceptance without substantive review, and any irregularities in the review record. Compromised review is a primary reason journals retract suspect papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inappropriate or irrelevant references
rubrics_metrics.description: References in a paper that are irrelevant or inappropriate for the work (journal noted 'inappropriate or irrelevant references').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check citation lists for irrelevant, self‑serving, or boilerplate references; excessive irrelevant citations may indicate manipulation to boost metrics or hide lack of substantive grounding. Corrections have removed 'irrelevant citations' in flagged papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Out-of-scope submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper content not being in scope for the publishing journal ('not being in scope of the journal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the topic, methods, and claims align with the journal's stated aims and scope. Publishing out‑of‑scope papers can indicate lax editorial standards or manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Massive self-citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive self‑citation by authors as a sign of suspicious behavior ('massive self-citation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate citation patterns for disproportionate self‑citation clusters, which may artificially inflate author metrics or be used by paper‑mill networks. Publishers may investigate and flag such patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known automated detection (Problematic Paper Screener)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of automated tools that comb literature for known fingerprints, improper synonym usage to evade plagiarism detectors, and misuse of generative AI (example: the Problematic Paper Screener scanning millions of articles weekly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage detector tools that search for recurring fingerprints, synonym/evasion patterns, and probable AI misuse. Maintain and review flagged lists (the article references a list of 78 flagged papers in one journal). Automated detection is one input for human investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper use of synonyms to evade plagiarism detectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors deliberately substitute synonyms or reword text to evade plagiarism detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for semantically identical but rephrased passages across papers, suspicious synonym patterns, and repeated rewording that preserves the same structure and data. Detection systems search specifically for these evasion techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misuse of generative AI or automated text tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Generation of text by language models or other automated tools that produces implausible or fabricated terminology, structure, or content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether odd phrasing, factual errors, or incoherent passages could stem from generative AI misuse. Investigate provenance of the text, and corroborate methods/results with raw data and human review.

rubrics_metrics.name: HTML vs PDF content discrepancies
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between HTML and PDF versions of a paper (example: phrase present in HTML abstract but not in the PDF).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare multiple versions and representations of the same paper; discrepancies may indicate post‑publication edits, conversion errors, or manipulation. Such mismatches can explain why some readers see suspect terms while others do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine‑reading/column-break artifact hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsense phrases may arise from faulty machine reading of scanned two‑column documents (e.g., 'vegetative' in left column vs 'electron microscopy' in right column read as one phrase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering odd compound phrases, examine original scanned sources and column layouts to see if line/column breaks were misinterpreted by OCR or AI training corpora. This can be an innocent origin or a mechanism exploited by paper mills/AI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation or transliteration errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistranslation or small script differences (example: Persian characters differing by a dot) that convert a legitimate term (like 'scanning electron microscopy') into a nonsense phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether language/translation errors could explain unusual wording, especially when flagged papers originate predominantly from a particular language/region. Consult native speakers and translation experts before concluding misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor as author / editorial conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior author or coauthor occupying an editorial role at the publishing journal (example: a senior author who is a special content editor at the journal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize submissions with editorial staff listed as authors for potential conflicts of interest, undue influence on editorial decisions, or lax review. Journals should disclose and manage such conflicts transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperprolific or controversial authorship patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors with extremely high publication rates or prior disciplinary actions (example: hyperprolific author suspended from institution) may be associated with problematic papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess author publication patterns, prior retractions/corrections, and reputation. Hyperprolific output, especially across disparate topics, can warrant deeper scrutiny of data and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of responsiveness / transparency from authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors failing to respond to editorial queries or requests for comment (several authors did not answer emails seeking comment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonresponse or evasiveness when asked for raw data, clarifications, or explanations should increase suspicion and may trigger investigations, expressions of concern, or retraction processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superficial peer review (reviewers not reading full text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers who only glance at titles and figures rather than reading full manuscripts, which can allow errors and paper‑mill products to pass review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reviewers are instructed and given time to read full manuscripts; editorial oversight should verify depth of review. Evidence that reviewers failed to engage deeply is a quality failure in the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial acceptance/justification of ambiguous wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may defend odd or shortened wording as acceptable (example: Editor‑in‑Chief saying the phrase conveys 'electron microscopy of vegetative structures').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial explanations for odd wording should be documented and justified; casual acceptance of unclear terms without correction can perpetuate confusion and allow problematic text to proliferate.
